newsitem.title: ISRAEL: No quick fix to Israel-PLO crisis - Netanyahu.
newsitem.headline: No quick fix to Israel-PLO crisis - Netanyahu.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu forecast on Sunday it would "take some time" before a U.S. Middle East envoy would be able to get Israel and the PLO to talk peace again.
PLO and Western officials said envoy Dennis Ross was trying to arrange a meeting of Israelis and Palestinians to discuss issues that led to the two-month-old freeze in peace negotiations.
Talks are stuck over Netanyahu's building of a Jewish settlement in disputed Jerusalem and a subsequent Israeli demand for a PLO crackdown on "terrorism".
Asked if Ross' second mission in a month was making progress, Netanyahu told Israel Radio: "Well I think that this is going to take some time. It's not happening overnight."

Ross returned to Jerusalem from Cairo on Saturday after meeting Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak. PLO officials said he would meet Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat at 10 p.m. (1900 GMT) in the West Bank city of Ramallah.
"Ross presented some ideas on how to restart contacts with Israel," a PLO official said.

"He suggested a meeting, not negotiations, between PLO and Israeli negotiators attended by Ross himself to probe into the issues that led to the crisis in the peace talks," said the official, who declined to be identified.
"Those issues are Israeli settlement activities including Jabal Abu Ghneim and Israeli violations in occupied Jerusalem."
Netanyahu started work in March on the 6,500-unit Har Homa Jewish settlement on Jabal Abu Ghneim, a hilltop in Arab East Jerusalem occupied in 1967. Both sides claim East Jerusalem.
Western officials said Ross was awaiting a response from Arafat on whether Palestinians would meet the Israelis. Arafat met his negotiating team in Ramallah on Saturday night.

Officials said the PLO was willing to meet the Israelis on condition the talks tackled the issues of Jewish settlements and Jerusalem and only after receiving U.S. guarantees the meeting would lead to a halt in settlement activities.
But Israeli officials said the meeting would have a different agenda -- not including Jewish settlement of occupied land.

Israeli government spokesman Moshe Fogel said: "In principle Israel didn't break off the talks, and we will raise issues that are of concern to us such as fighting terror and Palestinian violations to the agreement."

"We're not going to stop building in Jerusalem, we're not going to stop the natural growth of Jewish settlements," he said of Palestinian assertions the Jewish settlements on occupied Arab lands are a provocation.

Negotiations have been largely stalled since the start of the Jewish settlement and an attack on a Tel Aviv cafe in March that killed an Arab bomber and three Israelis. Palestinians refuse to resume talks until settlement activities are halted.
In the radio interview, Netanyahu repeated his vision of limited self-rule for Palestinians.

"They'll be able to choose their own institutions, elect their leaders, legislate their laws, levy their taxes, be independent in all the ways that are necessary for the conduct of their lives," he said.
"But certain powers would be shared and certain powers would be held by Israel, especially those powers that are necessary for the defence of our security," Netanyahu said.
